segments.narration_text:
March 1983. A newspaper in Calcutta runs a front-page story. India's spy chief, it says, has been working for the CIA. He has fled the country, through Kathmandu, with a suitcase of top-secret files.

Other papers follow. In Parliament, the Home Minister has to stand up and answer. The man, he says, is abroad. On a government assignment.

The story is false. According to B. Raman, a former R&AW colleague, it was planted by a disgruntled subordinate. The man at its centre is in the middle of a secret mission on Indira Gandhi's own request. Days later he returns, and retires on schedule, farewell party and all.

His name was N.F. Suntook. He ran R&AW for six years. And almost no one knows what he did. So how does the head of India's spy agency vanish from history? Everything here comes from B. Raman's own account, Indian journalism, and the few historians who have looked. It starts six years earlier, with a wrecked agency.

segments.label: SEGMENT 1
segments.title: THE ACCIDENTAL CHIEF
segments.visual_cue_raw: Dossier portrait — N.F. Suntook (silhouette; no photograph in the public record). The Indian Frontier Administrative Service.
segments.lower_third_text: N.F. Suntook · Indian Frontier Administrative Service · RAW chief, 1977–1983

paragraphs.text: Naushervan Framji Suntook was a Parsi. He was not a policeman. That alone made him unusual. Most of R&AW's leaders came from the Indian Police Service. Suntook came from the Indian Frontier Administrative Service, a cadre created to run the country's north-east. According to some accounts, he had also served in the Navy.

segments.narration_text:
Naushervan Framji Suntook was a Parsi. He was not a policeman. That alone made him unusual. Most of R&AW's leaders came from the Indian Police Service. Suntook came from the Indian Frontier Administrative Service, a cadre created to run the country's north-east. According to some accounts, he had also served in the Navy.

DailyO would later call him "an accidental chief." The description is fair. He was not the founder. He was not the visionary. He was the man who was in the room when everything fell apart.

There is no biography of Suntook. No interview. No known photograph. What survives is the story of six years.

segments.narration_text:
In March 1977, the Emergency ended. Indira Gandhi lost the election. Morarji Desai became Prime Minister. And Desai despised R&AW. Before the election, he had called it Indira Gandhi's "praetorian guard."

He did not abolish it. According to B. Raman, he cut it. The budget was trimmed. The staff was reduced. Some operations in neighbouring countries were stopped. And the leaders went.

Kao was pushed out in April. His deputy, K. Sankaran Nair, took over. Nair lasted about three months. He resigned rather than preside over the agency's downgrade. In his place, the government appointed Suntook, at a lower rank than Kao had held. DailyO would later call him a "pliable officer." It was not a compliment.

segments.narration_text:
For the next three years, Suntook did the least glamorous job in intelligence. He kept the building standing.

Yatish Yadav's history of R&AW puts it in one line. Desai, Yadav writes, put Suntook in charge. And somehow, Suntook "saved R&AW from being plundered by its own customer, the government." The customer was the Prime Minister.

According to B. Raman, the agency's files were reviewed by the new government's ministers. Home Minister Charan Singh, after going through the record, is reported to have told Kao that the allegations against R&AW had been wrong. It was a small vindication. It did not restore the budget.

The Janata government fell in 1979. In January 1980, Indira Gandhi returned to power. Kao came back as her security adviser. Now, R&AW's friends were in office again.

segments.narration_text:
By 1983, Suntook was due to retire. The date was March 31. A farewell party had been arranged. The evening before, Indira Gandhi called him in.

According to Raman, she asked for one last task, a sensitive mission to a friendly country. His service was extended by a few days. The party was postponed.

The country was Mauritius. It was in political turmoil. Prime Minister Anerood Jugnauth, a friend of India, faced a leftist rival whom Delhi distrusted. In Shashank Mattoo's account, Suntook worked with India's High Commissioner in Port Louis to help build a broad coalition of Indian-descent leaders around Jugnauth. Delhi had also drawn up contingency plans for a military response, Operation Lal Dora.

It did not come to that. In August 1983 Jugnauth won a decisive election, and Mauritius stayed close to India.

segments.narration_text:
Then the rumour hit. While Suntook was out of the country, a story spread that he had defected. The press did not retract it, even after the government raised the matter with the Press Council.

On April 7 he flew home. On April 8, according to Raman, he retired, and the farewell party went ahead. The nation's spy chief had been called a traitor on the day he was serving his country.

He retired to Gurgaon. His wife died in 1991. Raman writes that by 1993 he was ill, and alone. A newspaper ran a story about a forgotten spymaster. By 2004, Raman was calling him "the late N.F. Suntook."
